fields.foundation: The Oyo Empire began in the savannah woodlands of northern Yorubaland, north of the dense rainforest zone that made cavalry-based states difficult to form across much of coastal West Africa. Yoruba oral tradition attributes its founding to Oranmiyan, remembered as a son or grandson of Oduduwa, the mythical progenitor of the Yoruba people. He is said to have established the city of Oyo-Ile, also called Old Oyo or Katunga, as the dynasty’s sacred capital, probably in the fourteenth century. Oyo-Ile stood on open savannah, where horses could be used in war. Cavalry became the empire’s principal means of expansion and set Oyo apart from the forest Yoruba kingdoms to its south, where cavalry was of little use. The early centuries were precarious. Oyo was under constant pressure from the Nupe kingdom to the north-east and the Bariba of Borgu to the north-west, and in the early sixteenth century a crushing defeat by the Nupe forced the ruling dynasty into roughly eighty years of exile, much of it at Igboho. Exile strengthened Oyo’s military culture through sustained contact with the equestrian traditions of Borgu. The reoccupation of Oyo-Ile under Alaafin Abipa around 1610 opened the empire’s real period of expansion, as successive rulers extended Oyo’s tributary network westward and southward towards the Atlantic coast. King Agaja’s conquests of Allada and Ouidah upset the coastal trading order, and from 1726 onwards Oyo invaded Dahomey repeatedly. Dahomey was forced to pay tribute under Alaafin Ojigi, and a treaty of 1748 confirmed it as a tribute-paying vassal. Oyo was then at the height of its power, with a tributary network that extended from the Niger in the east across the Aja lands to the west and included Dahomey, Allada and Porto-Novo.
fields.socioeconomy: Oyo’s economy rested on its position on the trade routes that linked the Atlantic coast with the interior savannah and, beyond it, the Hausa states and trans-Saharan networks. European manufactures and other Atlantic imports passed through it in one direction, and the agricultural and pastoral products of the interior in the other. The empire drew substantial revenue from the tribute of subordinate states, Dahomey’s annual tribute including cloth, cowrie shells and enslaved persons, and from tolls on the long-distance caravans that crossed its territories. From the late seventeenth century onwards the Atlantic slave trade became more and more important to Oyo’s finances and its army. Captives taken in war and raids were sold to European merchants at coastal ports, particularly Ouidah, Porto-Novo and Badagry, in exchange for firearms, textiles and luxury goods that added to the prestige and military capacity of the Alaafin and the Oyo nobility. Farmers across the savannah heartland grew sorghum, millet and yams, which fed a dense population in walled towns and rural settlements governed by subordinate chiefs, while Oyo weavers and dyers produced cloth for regional markets. The cowrie shell was the standard currency and was accepted in markets across considerable distances. The Atlantic slave trade was profitable while the empire was expanding, but it created dependencies and depopulated parts of the region. These effects unsettled the tributary periphery and fed the instability of the late eighteenth century.
fields.military: Oyo’s military supremacy in the region rested above all on its cavalry, the most powerful horse-based force between the Niger and the Volta. The cavalry depended on the open savannah of the empire’s core and on a steady importation of horses from the north, since the tsetse-fly zones of the forest made horse-breeding impossible further south. The Eso, an elite body of seventy war chiefs serving the Alaafin, were the nucleus around which larger campaign forces were assembled. The Are-Ona-Kakanfo, the empire’s supreme field commander, was an appointed officer who, according to Oyo convention, was expected to win his campaigns or die in the attempt. Oyo armies made rapid, deep raids into enemy territory to seize captives, destroy the enemy’s economic resources and show that resistance was futile; they did not attempt the systematic occupation pursued by infantry-based empires. The Dahomey campaigns of the 1720s and 1730s showed how far this approach could reach and where it stopped. Oyo cavalry repeatedly devastated Dahomey but could not permanently hold its wooded southern territories, and Oyo settled for tribute rather than annexation. The empire’s great weakness was that its cavalry could not operate in the forest zones to the south. Coastal politics were therefore always managed through subordinate intermediaries rather than direct control, and this indirect relationship proved fragile when Dahomey under King Ghezo ceased paying tribute in the 1820s.
fields.governance: Oyo’s constitution was among the most developed in precolonial West Africa, and it balanced royal authority against aristocratic oversight. The Alaafin was a sacred king, in whose person divine Yoruba kingship was held to reside, and he ruled from the Afin, the royal palace at Oyo-Ile. In theory he held supreme authority, but he was constrained by the Oyo Mesi, a council of seven high chiefs headed by the Basorun. This council held the recognised power to reject an Alaafin judged to be ruling against the interests of the state. It signalled its decision by presenting an empty calabash or parrots’ eggs, after which the king was expected to take his own life. The mechanism was intended to prevent tyranny, but it was dangerously open to abuse. During the ascendancy of Basorun Gaa, from about 1754 to 1774, the Basorun is said to have driven several successive Alaafins to their deaths and effectively ruled the empire himself, until Alaafin Abiodun built a coalition, with the support of the Are-Ona-Kakanfo Oyabi, that overthrew and executed him around 1774. In the provinces subordinate rulers governed under the supervision of the Ajele, royal agents stationed in tributary towns, whose exactions caused chronic resentment in the periphery. The Ogboni society, a religious and judicial association representing the earth cult and the free citizens, was a further counterweight. It mediated disputes and maintained social cohesion independently of the palace.
fields.impact: Oyo’s widest effect on the world came through the Atlantic slave trade, in which it was a central participant in the triangular commerce connecting West Africa, the Americas and Europe during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Oyo-controlled trade networks are estimated to have contributed several hundred thousand captives to the Atlantic trade. The wars that followed the empire’s collapse sent still larger numbers of Yoruba-speaking captives to the Americas in the early nineteenth century, above all to Brazil, particularly Bahia, and to Cuba. Their religious practices became foundational to Candomblé in Brazil and Santería (Lucumí) in Cuba, while Yoruba, or Nago, elements also entered Haitian Vodou alongside its predominantly Fon and Kongo roots. Within the region, Oyo’s sustained pressure on Dahomey affected the political development of the entire Bight of Benin coast, and the empire’s collapse displaced very large numbers of people and changed the demographic and political geography of what is now south-western Nigeria. Refugees and warriors from the Oyo heartland founded or enlarged new centres such as Ibadan, Abeokuta and Ijaye, which became the leading Yoruba powers of the nineteenth century. Oyo keeps a large place in Yoruba cultural memory. Its constitutional ideas and traditions of sacred kingship informed Yoruba political thought and identity long after the empire itself ceased to exist.
fields.decline: Oyo collapsed in a short period between about 1790 and 1836, under the combined effects of constitutional dysfunction, military overextension, provincial resentment and religious and military pressure from outside. The Basorun Gaa crisis had damaged the legitimacy of the Oyo Mesi and left lasting mistrust between the Alaafin and the military aristocracy. Alaafin Abiodun’s long reign (c. 1770–1789) brought stability but favoured Atlantic commercial revenues over military strength, and the army deteriorated as external threats grew. Around 1796, Alaafin Awole was rejected and forced to take his own life after the Are-Ona-Kakanfo Afonja and other chiefs mutinied against his order to attack Iwere, a town under the Alaafin’s own sacred protection. The mutiny broke the compact between king and military elite. Around 1817 Afonja, based at Ilorin, rebelled openly and enlisted the support of the Fulani Muslim cleric Alimi and Hausa and Fulani followers inspired by the Sokoto jihad, which brought a dangerous new enemy into the centre of the empire. Afonja was himself killed by his allies in the early 1820s, and Ilorin became an emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its reformist Islamic ideology rejected Oyo’s sacred kingship, and its persistent military pressure, combined with internal fragmentation and Dahomey’s secession, made the empire’s position untenable. Oyo-Ile fell and was abandoned around 1835–1836. Alaafin Atiba then established a reduced successor state at New Oyo further south, which signed a treaty with the British in 1888 and was later absorbed into colonial Nigeria, where the Alaafin’s office survived as a traditional kingship.
fields.summary: The Oyo Empire’s historical significance is most visible in the African diaspora it helped to create. Yoruba language, religion and cultural practice were carried across the Atlantic world and became living traditions in Brazil and Cuba. An empire that profited from the slave trade, and was in the end overwhelmed by the wars that fed it, is remembered in the societies built by its victims.
fields.teaser: The Oyo Empire was the dominant Yoruba state and one of West Africa's most powerful kingdoms, with a constitutional system that could depose an unpopular ruler.
fields.t0: The Oyo Empire was a Yoruba savannah state whose cavalry made it the leading power between the Niger and the Volta.
fields.t1: It grew rich on tribute and the Atlantic slave trade, forcing Dahomey into vassalage and shaping the Bight of Benin coast.
fields.t2: Feuds between king and chiefs, Afonja's revolt and the Ilorin emirate destroyed it; Oyo-Ile was abandoned c. 1835–1836.
fields.dyk: Oyo's council of chiefs could reject an Alaafin by presenting him with an empty calabash or parrots' eggs, after which the king was expected to take his own life.
